creator: Jacob Rees-Mogg
title: Cryptocurrency: criminal or common sense?
full_text:
The very large donations that have been
made to reform 72 million pounds have
raised questions once again about
cryptocurrency.
Are they just a means of criminals
moving cash about useful for drug
traders and money launderers and
Russians? Or are they in fact a very
useful and interesting part of the new
economic environment?
I changed my mind on this. I think about
it carefully. I think it's very
important. But I had a very interesting
discussion last week with Arthur
Laugher, which I'm putting up on YouTube
via GB News and we'll have the
highlights of the interview on my GB
News program.
When I was discussing it with Arthur
Laugher, what he pointed out to me was
that dollar bills are used by criminals,
pound notes are used by fraudsters,
currency is always used by criminals. Of
course it is because they get paid for
their crime. They steal something and
they sell it to get cash. They sell
drugs and they get cash. There was an
incident few years ago when HSBC took in
millions of dollars in a bank just
across the border into Mexico from the
United States which came to them in
suitcases of cash. This was long after
anti-moneylaundering rules were
introduced and it made it a bit rum when
all of us have to go through the ninth
degree or whatever degree it is to open
a bank account when HSBC was at that
point taking any amount of cash from
obvious criminals. So any form of
currency can be used for criminality.
If you put that to one side and you say,
well actually cryptocurrency is not
simply a mechanism of supporting crime,
then it becomes a really interesting
form of money. What is money? We've
discussed this before, but money is a
store of value, a means of exchange, and
a form of account. Those are the three
qualities that money has to meet. But
fiat currency, that is to say, currency
that is not based on anything, has never
remained a store of value. It's been
essentially a fraud that people thought
that they had a store of value with a
pound note, a£5 note, or a $5 bill, but
they found that its value was
consistently eroded by inflation.
Between 1690 and 1914,
the value of a pound remained steady.
There was inflation and there was
deflation. But if you had a pound in
1690, it would buy a pound's worth of
goods in 1914.
This is really quite extraordinary in
the modern context where a pound, if you
had it in 1914, would now be worth less
than a penny. The devaluation through
inflation has been
effectively to wipe out the value of
currency. So [snorts] modern fiat
currencies are not a store of value.
They are a means of exchange and they
are a unit of account. Cryptocurrency
at the moment is different. It's been a
speculative investment
rather than a currency.
Logically, a currency's value ought to
remain relatively stable, other things
being equal, that if it buys a pound
today, it should buy a pound tomorrow.
There are factors that may change its
value over time relating to inflation,
but there's been a huge amount of
speculative interest in
cryptocurrencies.
There are various types of
cryptocurrencies.
Some of them are a racket and you should
avoid like the plague. The ones that are
interesting are stable currencies where
the issuance is limited because this
gets over the problem of inflation.
Inflation comes about as a monetary
phenomenon that if you create an
increase in supply of currency then the
value of the currency will decline. This
is why governments can't just print
money to pay for all the goods and
services that people want. they have to
take it in taxation. If they were just
to print it, you would soon have
hyperinflation and currency would lose
all its value. Instead, what they've
done is printed currency on the margin.
Quantive easing was printing money.
Hence, we had a strong inflation uh in
the early 2020s postcoid as the
consequences of that printing of money
came home to roost. So stable currencies
that limit the amount that they issue
are less likely to suffer from
inflation. Indeed, they should not
suffer from inflation. And that makes
them an interesting store of value over
the long term. [snorts] They are not yet
particularly a means of exchange. People
accept them but then change them into
currencies, but that can happen because
of market forces, but they are
definitely not a unit of account.
Now when we think of all this and we
think that cryptocurrencies have been a
speculation, it reminds me of the South
Sea bubble because the South Sea bubble
was a speculation on something that had
a genuine value but that that value got
ex distorted out of all sensible
proportion.
There was the prospect of trade in the
South Seas, but it had the underlying
value of government debt. It had bought
guilts and these guilts instead of
trading at their real value traded at
enormous premium as people wanted to get
into the excitement of the South Sea.
That has happened with cryptocurrencies.
People have wanted to be in
cryptocurrencies
and therefore [snorts] they have bought
them at inflated prices because
new ones weren't being created and that
meant that the supply was limited.
Demand to get into them was very high.
That seems to me to be the opening salvo
of a developing economic activity that
you get bubbles when things are new.
people get over excited about them,
irrationally exuberant, which I think
was um Alan Greenspan's phrase for what
happens when markets get out of kilter.
But that doesn't change the underlying
issue. And this is why governments hate
it.
Governments hate cryptocurrency
because it takes away their ability to
debortch the currency. And governments
that have the ability to debortch the
currency always do.
Think of this. If inflation were at its
target of 2%. On the assumption that
factors of 70 double every 35 years your
money halves in value.
If on the other hand they don't achieve
that target and instead inflation is at
3 12% the value of your money halves
every 20 years. Now, this is fantastic
for governments because they issue
government debt today at 100% of GDP.
And if they managed to run a balanced
budget for 20 years at 3 and a half%
inflation and nothing else happened, the
debt would be 50% of GDP. It's a
fantastic way of taking money from
people without them noticing. It's not
free money. It's not just accounting
money. That is a cost you have to bear
as a loss of value as the government
takes it from you. [snorts] But it's
much less painful than putting on an
income tax, VAT or other forms of
taxation. And governments have done this
throughout history. If you read Jonathan
Sumption's wonderful series of books on
the hundred years war, you will see that
in the early stages, the main way in
which the French crown funded itself was
by devaluing the currency and reissuing
it with slightly less precious metal
inside, taking the rest and using that
to fund the war. It was essentially an
expropriation without a formal taxation.
Printing money is the same thing. It is
what governments do. But cryptocurrency,
stable currency stops is happening and
therefore governments are very nervous
of stable currency and they want to stop
it. They want to regulate it other than
Donald Trump because they want power and
control. So interestingly, it seems to
me that cryptocurrency
is going to be the answer to the state
running more and more of our lives that
it will settle down. It will cease to be
a speculation. It will have real value
as long as it's stable currency with
limited issuance, possibly backed by
gold or something real and tangible. And
you won't make a lot of money out of it,
but you won't be robbed by the
government year in year out. And that's
why governments say it's criminal and
all these things because they're
frightened of it. The voter, the
individual, the consumer should be
thinking very seriously about whether it
will be a better form of money than the
notes that we get today have no
intrinsic value. As always, thank you
very much for watching.

notes.note: Fixed-supply currencies can still suffer high price inflation. When goods are priced in Bitcoin, capped at 21 million, its inflation rate has dwarfed U.S. dollar inflation and swung between inflation and deflation because fixed supply cannot adjust to demand.
notes.claim: Stable currencies that limit issuance do not suffer from inflation.
notes.context_quote: So stable currencies that limit the amount that they issue are less likely to suffer from inflation. Indeed, they should not suffer from inflation.
notes.context_paragraph: So stable currencies that limit the amount that they issue are less likely to suffer from inflation. Indeed, they should not suffer from inflation. And that makes them an interesting store of value over the long term.

sources.quote: Even our currently high inflation rate in U.S. dollars is dwarfed by the towering peaks of the inflation rate in Bitcoin—not to mention Bitcoin’s wild gyrations.
sources.explanation: Shows Bitcoin-priced inflation was much higher than dollar inflation with wild swings.

sources.quote: Never in the history of the U.S. dollar has the inflation rate reached the heights that Bitcoin has on several occasions in a few years.
sources.explanation: Shows Bitcoin has reached inflation heights never seen for the dollar.
Shows Bitcoin also swings to deflation, supporting inflation-deflation swings.

sources.quote: Bitcoin is similar in that it also has a more-or-less fixed quantity that cannot respond to fluctuations in demand.
sources.explanation: Explains fixed supply cannot adjust to demand, causing price fluctuations.

sources.quote: With no means to manage the supply of dollars, there was no way to avoid fluctuations in price when the demand for money fluctuated.
sources.explanation: Links fixed supply to inability to avoid price fluctuations when demand changes.

notes.note: New Bitcoin are still being created via mining. Miners currently receive 3.125 BTC per block about every 10 minutes, with roughly 19.95 million BTC already issued and about 1.05 million still left to issue before the 21 million cap is reached.
notes.claim: Cryptocurrency supply was limited because new coins were not being created.
notes.context_quote: because new ones weren't being created and that meant that the supply was limited. Demand to get into them was very high.
notes.context_paragraph: People have wanted to be in cryptocurrencies and therefore [snorts] they have bought them at inflated prices because new ones weren't being created and that meant that the supply was limited. Demand to get into them was very high.

sources.quote: At this stage in Bitcoin's lifecycle, the network's daily issuance rate stands at approximately 450 new Bitcoins.
sources.explanation: Shows new coins are still entering circulation daily via mining.

sources.quote: In 2026, the Bitcoin block reward remains 3.125 BTC per block, a level set by the April 2024 halving.
sources.explanation: Confirms the current reward amount claimed in the note.

sources.quote: The network's difficulty automatically recalibrates every 2,016 blocks, roughly two weeks, to maintain an average block creation time of 10 minutes.
sources.explanation: Confirms blocks average about every 10 minutes.

sources.quote: As of 2026, approximately 20.01 million BTC have been mined, representing over 95% of Bitcoin's total fixed supply.
sources.explanation: Confirms ~20M mined, consistent with roughly 19.95M in note.

sources.quote: As of 2026, less than 987,000 BTC remain to be mined before reaching Bitcoin's hard cap of 21 million.
sources.explanation: Confirms ~1M left to mine up to the 21M hard cap.

sources.quote: The protocol has a hardcoded total supply of 21 million BTC, a fixed upper limit that cannot be changed without a consensus-breaking update.

Bitcoin's protocol caps total issuance at 21 million BTC, enforced by a halving subsidy schedule in Bitcoin Core's GetBlockSubsidy function (source: [GitHub](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/src/validation.cpp)).
As of April 2026 roughly 19.95 million BTC have been issued (~95% of the cap), leaving ~1.05 million for ~115 more years of decaying issuance.
sources.explanation: Directly confirms roughly 19.95M issued and ~1.05M left.

sources.quote: Current era (5th) pays 3.125 BTC per block since the April 2024 halving at block 840,000; ~450 BTC issued per day, ~164,000 per year; next halving to 1.5625 BTC expected around April 2028 at block 1,050,000
sources.explanation: Confirms miners get 3.125 BTC per block and new issuance continues.

sources.quote: Difficulty adjusts every 2,016 blocks to target ten-minute intervals, but real intervals are Poisson-distributed and often run slightly faster than target.
sources.explanation: Confirms blocks target ten-minute intervals, i.e. about every 10 minutes.
